Thank you, Cynthia, and good morning to all. So I will also focus more on the Convention 193 rather than the larger issue of AI. It was a testament to the enduring relevance of tripartism, because we had very difficult conversations for at least over two years, and in June of 2003, a very, very difficult conversation. But in the end, the committee adopted the convention by consensus. That was very important, adopted by consensus. So it shows that it is possible, but it also shows the extreme relevance of international labor standards in a changing world of work. Because this convention is about the future of work. It is about regulating issues such as algorithmic management. It is about regulating issues which were not done in the past. And one of the reasons we could do it, and I think Kathy made a very important point about the fact that innovation does not necessarily need deregulation, can go here. The reason that was possible was because of what you, Jackie, said about the balance. So this convention managed to achieve the balance between the job creating potential of the platform economy, because indeed it creates lots of jobs for young people. It can aid formalization because of traceability. It also gives the chance to many people who are usually marginalized, such as refugees and migrants, workers with disabilities, and even women who want to balance family work with care work. So there are many positives, but at the same time, there are two concerns and huge challenges about protection and rights of work. So the convention recognizes the positive elements, the potential of job creation, but at the same time it addresses those issues in relation to protecting workers, wages, remuneration, payment, social security, protection of data, protection against violence and harassment, also human involvement in decisions that relate to automated decision making. So all these issues are also taken care of. Now, No way. It is about. And I also want to make this clear that this convention is not about regulating technology. It doesn't regulate technology. What it regulates is the impact of technology. Access to work and on conditions to work, and I think this distinction is very important. Now going forward, of course it provides an excellent benchmark to the international community. It also, in a way, translates the. centenary declaration of the ILO in 2019, which spoke about a human-centered approach to technology. It also provides a very good benchmark to the global digital compact, which is about also having a human-centered approach to technology. But the question now is implementing it. And in implementing it, of course, they are working with countries and there is a lot of interest. But the actual implementation of it will require very robust labor market information systems. But it can also be based on the four pillars of the decent work agenda. That is promoting job creation, skills. Skills will be a very important part of it. Enterprise development, as in support for SMEs, along with the protection of workers, social security, wages, protection against violence. Social dialogue, I think everybody has mentioned, is what brought us here today. But we need to continue with that at the country level and at the global level. And the question of fundamental principles and rights at work. And I also want to say that this convention not only recognizes the importance of respecting, promoting, and realizing fundamental principles and rights at work, but also in the context of automated decision-making and algorithmic which were very difficult discussions, but in the end, we got there. I see the end goal. And in terms of going forward, international cooperation, it's a great benchmark. And it also shows that international labor standards will continue to be an important instrument in regulating the world of work in the context of the various changes that we are seeing. And who knows what change we will see in the coming years. I mean, the change that's happening is so fast, at least we have a basis And the convention is very principles-based, but it allows space for change, and it leaves a lot of very detailed decisions to the member states. It does not specify every single detail, except of the broad context. With that, over to you, Secretary. Thank you.

It has also been a point of reference for the Pope Leo's intervention today at UNESCO headquarters in Paris. So indeed, very happy to be engaged with everyone today. I have to start first from UNESCO to say that we really welcome the adoption of the Convention 193. A landmark achievement that comes at a time when robust normality frameworks and most importantly their implementation is essential to advancing sustainable and inclusive development, particularly important because digital platforms are not mere workplaces. Indeed, for millions of people around the world, they represent the first point of entry into the labor market. And I have here with me the statistics, apparently between 150 and 435 million people engage in online gig work worldwide, and the majority of them being under the age of 30. 6 in 10 living outside major urban cities. So indeed, this is not a niche phenomenon. It is a gateway to employment opportunity and livelihood for entire generations. So let me share just a few points from UNESCO. First, first for us is the need to bring education and training authorities more systematically into the social dialogue on the platform. The education community faces a profound challenge: how to prepare learners for a future in which many of the jobs they hold do not exist. So, this is why the dialogue on skills cannot remain confined to labour institutions, employers, and workers. It has to systematically include education systems, and training systems should also have a seat at the table. Labour stakeholders, of course, can signal what is changing in the world of work, but it is the education system that's going to translate that into the curriculum, qualifications, teachers' development, and finally into the assessments. And of course, today, this transformation must include AI skills. So we have certain tools at UNESCO that we've developed, like you just mentioned briefly, UNESCO's AI competency frameworks for students and teachers, but combined technical understandings with ethics and human-centered mindset. Second, is the importance to invest in AI literacy, as I said, media and information literacy. but also TVET and lifelong learning. And to make sure that skills gained through the new forms of the work are recognized and can be carried forward. So indeed, the issue of the recognition. Of course, the platform work is inherently global, and we know that the worker in Nairobi may be serving a client in Berlin, from a platform registered in a third country. Our labour standards and protections generally apply where the worker is based. The problem is that again, the qualifications and the skills rarely travel as easily across borders. So as a result, There is a need for a qualification recognized across the border and UNESCO has a tool, the UNESCO Global Convention on Recognition of Qualifications. Let me run through very fast to my last point, certainly to mention that ethics and governance is quite important. None of what we have discussed today can rest on individual skills and capabilities. It depends on how the platforms and technologies shaping the future of work are governed. And here, UNESCO has done, has led on the global agreement, there are UNESCO recommendations on ethics of artificial intelligence that places, of course, human dignity at the center of the entire AI life cycle. And this cannot be an afterthought. Definitely, technology should not risk reinforcing existing inequalities, but should rather reduce them. And I have to say that our normative work fully aligns with the normative work of our sister agency, with the ILO's Convention 193. And it's definitely a solid normative framework that can help each one of us contribute to a more inclusive digital future. Thank you.
